title: The Rebound Effect
equation: Total Use = (Tasks × Use per Task) ÷ Efficiency
hook: You bought the tool to save time. Somehow you're busier than ever.
statement: Make something cheaper or faster to use and you'll usually end up using a lot more of it.
explainer: Efficiency drops the cost per task, so you take on more tasks. Total use goes up even as each one gets leaner. That's why faster tools almost never hand you free time.
sop: Pick one recent efficiency win, like a new tool or automation.
Note your Tasks and Use per Task from before.
Estimate how many more tasks the lower cost will pull in.
Calculate Total Use with the new Efficiency.
Decide on purpose what the freed-up capacity is for.
equation_example: Before: (100 tasks × 5 units) ÷ 1 = 500 units. Efficiency doubles and tasks jump to 500: (500 × 5) ÷ 2 = 1,250 units. Total use went up, not down. Only weak demand would let it fall.
question: Write down one tool that saved you time, and what actually filled that time.
closing_statement: Efficiency only frees you if you choose what to do with it.
caption:
Principle Nº 338: The Rebound Effect

You bought the tool to save time. Somehow you're busier than ever.

Make something cheaper or faster to use and you'll usually end up using a lot more of it.
